course.title: Complete SQLite Masterclass
course.tagline: SQLite 3.53 from zero to embedded production, one module at a time.
course.standard: SQLite 3.53 baseline; version-specific features are labelled.
course.description: Module 00 builds the SQLite mental model: embedded, serverless, single-file storage, type affinity, keys and how a prepared statement becomes rows.
outcomes: Explain why SQLite is embedded and serverless
Read an SQLite schema and name rows, columns and keys
Distinguish SQLite from MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server
Trace a query through parse, bytecode and B-tree access

modules.title: Introduction to SQLite
modules.goal: Build the SQLite mental model: one file, no server, real SQL.

topics.title: What Is SQLite?
topics.simple: SQLite ek chhota database engine hai jo aapke app ke andar hi chalta hai — alag server ki zaroorat nahi.
topics.pro: SQLite is an embedded, serverless relational database engine that stores an entire database in a single cross-platform file and links directly into the application.
points: It is the most widely deployed database engine.

topics.title: What Is a Database?
topics.simple: Database data ka organised collection hai jise query karke padha aur badla ja sakta hai.
topics.pro: A database is an organised collection of structured data managed by an engine that enforces types, constraints and transactions.
points: Queries turn stored data into answers.

topics.title: Why Do We Need Databases?
topics.simple: Spreadsheet ki copies bhejne se confusion hota hai; database ek saaf source of truth deta hai.
topics.pro: Databases centralise data, avoid duplication, enforce integrity and support concurrent access and durable writes.

example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS students FROM students;

topics.title: What Is SQL?
topics.simple: SQL wo language hai jisse hum database se sawaal poochte hain aur data badalte hain.
topics.pro: SQL is the declarative language used to define, query and modify relational data; SQLite implements a large subset of it.
points: SQLite supports SELECT, JOIN, CTE and window functions.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: What Is a Relational Database?
topics.simple: Relational database data ko tables me rakhta hai aur keys se tables ko jodta hai.
topics.pro: A relational database represents data as relations (tables) and relationships through primary and foreign keys.
points: Rows are records, columns are typed attributes.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;

topics.title: What Makes SQLite Different?
topics.simple: SQLite server nahi hai — yeh library hai jo app ke andar database file padhti hai.
topics.pro: SQLite is a library, not a client-server service: the application links it and reads/writes the database file directly.
points: No users, roles or network listener.
Concurrency is file-level with WAL helping readers.

topics.title: SQLite vs MySQL
topics.simple: SQLite file-based aur embedded hai; MySQL server-based hai aur kai users ko network par serve karta hai.
topics.pro: SQLite is embedded and serverless; MySQL is a client-server RDBMS with users, roles, network access and multiple storage engines.
points: MySQL has server processes and ports.
SQLite is ideal for local apps and tests.

topics.title: SQLite vs PostgreSQL
topics.simple: SQLite chhota aur simple hai; PostgreSQL bada server hai advanced types aur extensions ke saath.
topics.pro: SQLite is an embedded engine with dynamic typing; PostgreSQL is a server RDBMS with strict types, roles, extensions and richer SQL.
points: SQLite uses type affinity; PostgreSQL uses strict types.
Both support transactions, joins and CTEs.

topics.title: SQLite vs SQL Server
topics.simple: SQLite app ke andar chalta hai; SQL Server Microsoft ka bada server database hai.
topics.pro: SQLite is an embedded file-based engine; SQL Server is a Microsoft client-server RDBMS with T-SQL, roles and enterprise administration.
points: SQL Server needs a service and authentication.
SQLite is far smaller to deploy.

topics.title: SQLite vs NoSQL
topics.simple: SQLite tables aur SQL use karta hai; NoSQL flexible documents ya key-value stores use karta hai.
topics.pro: SQLite is relational and SQL-based; NoSQL systems trade joins and strict schemas for flexible documents, key-value or graph models.
points: NoSQL may scale horizontally more easily.
Choose by access pattern and integrity needs.

topics.title: What Is an Embedded Database?
topics.simple: Embedded database app ke saath ship hota hai — alag server install nahi karna padta.
topics.pro: An embedded database is linked into the application process and stores data locally, with no separate server to install or administer.
points: Backup means copying the file safely.

topics.title: What Is a Serverless Database?
topics.simple: Serverless ka matlab yahan alag database server process nahi hai — SQLite library hi engine hai.
topics.pro: SQLite is serverless in the architectural sense: there is no long-running database server; the library reads and writes the file in-process.
points: The app opens the file directly.

topics.title: What Is a Self-Contained Database?
topics.simple: SQLite database ek hi file me tables, indexes aur data — sab kuch le kar chalta hai.
topics.pro: A self-contained SQLite database stores its schema, data, indexes and metadata in one cross-platform file with a stable format.
points: WAL mode adds sidecar files while open.

topics.title: SQLite Real-World Applications
topics.simple: SQLite phones, browsers, desktop apps aur embedded devices me data store karne ke liye common hai.
topics.pro: SQLite powers mobile app storage, browser internals, desktop applications, embedded devices, local caches and test suites.
points: Android and iOS apps use it.
Browsers use it for internal stores.

topics.title: SQLite in Desktop Applications
topics.simple: Desktop app apne data ko local SQLite file me rakh sakta hai — offline bhi kaam karta hai.
topics.pro: Desktop applications embed SQLite for local documents, settings, caches and offline-first data, avoiding a server dependency.
points: One file per document or app.

topics.title: SQLite in Mobile Applications
topics.simple: Mobile apps SQLite me local data rakhte hain taaki network ke bina bhi UI chale.
topics.pro: Android and iOS ship SQLite for local relational storage; apps use it for caches, messages, offline records and sync queues.
points: No server install on the device.

topics.title: SQLite in Browsers and Embedded Devices
topics.simple: Browser aur chhote devices SQLite ko WASM ya embedded library ke roop me chalate hain.
topics.pro: SQLite compiles to WebAssembly for browser labs and runs on embedded devices where a server is impossible.
points: SQLite WASM runs in this app’s SQL Lab.
No native install needed in the browser.
The same SQL core runs locally.

topics.title: SQLite Advantages
topics.simple: SQLite chhota, fast, reliable aur zero-config hai — file copy karo aur database le jao.
topics.pro: SQLite offers zero-configuration deployment, a single-file database, ACID transactions, broad platform support and a very small footprint.
points: Excellent for local and embedded use.

topics.title: SQLite Limitations
topics.simple: SQLite multi-user server nahi hai; ek waqt me ek writer, no roles, no stored procedures.
topics.pro: SQLite has no built-in users/roles, no stored procedures, limited concurrency (one writer) and is not designed for network filesystems.
points: No native FULL OUTER JOIN before 3.39.

topics.title: When Should We Use SQLite?
topics.simple: Jab data local ho, app embedded ho, aur simple reliable storage chahiye — SQLite best hai.
topics.pro: Use SQLite for local apps, mobile storage, embedded devices, caches, test databases and single-user or read-heavy workloads.

topics.title: When Should We Avoid SQLite?
topics.simple: Jab kai network users ek saath likh rahe hon ya server-style roles chahiye hon, tab MySQL/PostgreSQL better hai.
topics.pro: Avoid SQLite for high-concurrency multi-writer services, network-shared files, strict server roles or workloads needing stored procedures.

topics.title: SQLite Database File
topics.simple: SQLite database ek file hai — usme pages hote hain jinme tables aur indexes rehte hain.
topics.pro: A SQLite database is a paged file with a header, B-tree pages for tables and indexes, a freelist and optional WAL/journal sidecars.
points: The file is portable across platforms.
Pages are the unit of I/O.
WAL adds -wal and -shm files while open.

topics.title: How SQLite Executes Queries
topics.simple: SQLite query ko parse karta hai, bytecode banata hai, virtual machine se chalata hai aur rows lautata hai.
topics.pro: SQLite parses SQL, prepares a bytecode program, runs it on its virtual machine and returns rows through the prepared statement API.
points: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the access path.

example.sql: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: SQLite Architecture
topics.simple: SQLite ka core library SQL ko parse karke B-tree pages par read/write karta hai — sab app ke process me.
topics.pro: SQLite’s architecture layers the SQL compiler, bytecode virtual machine, B-tree and pager over the OS file, all inside the application process.
points: The pager manages pages and locking.

interview.q: What is data, and how does it differ from information?
interview.answer: Data is a raw recorded value; information is data organised and interpreted in context. A database stores data, and a query turns it into information.

interview.q: Why do we need a database?
interview.answer: To keep one durable source of truth, enforce integrity, support concurrent access and make large datasets queryable through indexes and SQL.
Software that defines, stores, queries, secures and recovers databases. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite are DBMSs.
A DBMS based on the relational model: data lives in tables, keys declare relationships and SQL is the query language.
Every RDBMS is a DBMS, but an RDBMS adds relations, keys, joins and referential integrity. A DBMS may use other models.
Structured Query Language, the declarative language for defining, querying and modifying relational data.
You describe the result you want; the optimiser chooses the execution plan. That separates intent from physical access paths.
SQL is the standard language; MySQL is an RDBMS product that implements it with its own dialect, storage engines and functions.
SQL is the language; PostgreSQL is an RDBMS known for standards compliance, rich types, transactions and extensions.
SQL is the language; SQLite is an embedded, serverless RDBMS stored in one file, ideal for local tools and tests.
SQL databases are relational and schema-first; NoSQL systems trade joins and strict integrity for flexible documents, key-value or graph models.
A relation: a named set of typed columns holding rows. Constraints on the table protect data quality.
One record in a table, containing one value per column. Rows are unordered unless a query sorts them.
A named attribute with a data type shared by every row. Column names should be stable and descriptive.
They are effectively the same in a relational table: a record is the logical entry, a row is its physical representation.
A column is the whole named attribute across rows; a field is one value at a specific row-column intersection.
The logical structure of the database: tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and relationships, often grouped under a schema name.
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL. It is usually indexed and referenced by foreign keys.
A column or set of columns whose values must match a candidate key in another table, enforcing referential integrity.

interview.q: How is a SQL query executed?
interview.answer: The engine parses and validates it, the optimiser chooses a plan, and the executor reads or writes storage and returns rows or a command status.

labs.title: Select every column
labs.task: Return every column and row from students.
labs.solution: SELECT * FROM students;

labs.title: Select two columns
labs.task: Return name and marks from students.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students;
labs.expected: name and marks for every student.

labs.title: Filter by marks
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

labs.title: Sort by marks
labs.task: Return name and marks sorted highest first.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;
labs.expected: Rows from highest to lowest marks.

labs.title: Count rows
labs.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM students;

labs.title: Distinct cities
labs.solution: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students;

labs.title: Average marks
labs.solution: SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg_marks FROM students;

labs.title: Group by city
labs.solution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students GROUP BY city;

labs.title: Join courses
labs.task: Return student name and course title.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN courses c ON c.id = s.course_id;
labs.expected: One row per matching student-course pair.

labs.title: Top three
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;

labs.title: Filter and sort
labs.task: Return students in Pune sorted by name.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune' ORDER BY name;

labs.title: Between values
labs.task: Return students with marks between 60 and 90.
labs.solution: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

labs.title: Pattern match
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

labs.title: Null check
labs.task: Return students whose city is missing.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city IS NULL;

labs.title: Alias a column
labs.solution: SELECT marks AS score FROM students;

labs.title: Calculated column
labs.solution: SELECT marks + 5 AS boosted FROM students;

labs.title: Maximum marks
labs.solution: SELECT MAX(marks) AS top FROM students;

labs.title: Minimum marks
labs.solution: SELECT MIN(marks) AS low FROM students;

labs.title: Group with HAVING
labs.task: Return cities with more than one student.
labs.solution: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
labs.expected: Cities with at least two students.

labs.title: Subquery maximum
labs.task: Return the student with the highest marks.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks = (SELECT MAX(marks) FROM students);

logic.q: Why does SELECT * return columns in table order?
logic.answer: The table definition fixes column order; SELECT * expands to that order unless the query lists columns explicitly.

logic.q: Why can a primary key not be NULL?
logic.answer: A NULL cannot identify a row uniquely, so the key would fail its purpose.

logic.q: Why does a foreign key prevent orphan rows?
logic.answer: It requires each value to match a key in the referenced table, or be NULL if allowed.
The query states the desired result; the optimiser chooses the execution plan.
To reduce redundancy and avoid insert, update and delete anomalies.

logic.q: Why can two rows have the same name?
logic.answer: A name is not a key unless declared unique; only the primary key must be unique.

logic.q: Why does ORDER BY matter for LIMIT?
logic.answer: Without ORDER BY, LIMIT returns an arbitrary set; ORDER BY defines which rows are “top”.

logic.q: Why does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)?
logic.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULL values in that column.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the remaining rows are grouped and aggregated.
It filters groups after aggregation, which WHERE cannot do.

logic.q: Why is a schema separate from data?
logic.answer: The schema is the structure; data is the content stored within that structure.

logic.q: Why do joins need a matching key?
logic.answer: The key defines which rows from each table belong together.

logic.q: Why can an index speed up a query?
logic.answer: It lets the engine find rows without scanning the whole table.

logic.q: Why can too many indexes hurt?
logic.answer: Every write must maintain them, adding storage and latency.

logic.q: Why is SQL portable but not identical everywhere?
logic.answer: The core language is standardised, but dialects differ in types, functions and extensions.
